episodes.202622: A line of storms moving across Converse and Niobrara Counties produced strong winds and frequent lightning.
episodes.202668: A broken line of thunderstorms moved across Washington and Lincoln Counties producing wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph.
episodes.203723: Thunderstorms on the Fourth of July produced a strong wind gust with the Aberdeen Regional Airport Automated Surface Observing System reaching a peak of 81 mph. Heavy rainfall from these storms also led to flash flooding in Aberdeen and later in Watertown.
episodes.203928: A shortwave trough initiated cluster of storms coming out of Colorado. Once these storms developed a cold pool, it transitioned to a more linear structure. The storms produced some severe wind gusts and wind damage.
episodes.203929: A partially cutoff low ejected through the region through early July, followed by a weaker trailing shortwave trough. This unsettled pattern resulted in sporadic instances of strong to severe wind gusts in addition to hail.
episodes.203932: A shortwave moving through the area resulted in the development of late afternoon to evening convection. This convection was fairly high based in nature, resulting in strong outflow winds in turn.
episodes.204145: In the late afternoon of the 4th, a line of thunderstorms swept across northeastern Colorado. In the early evening, as these storms moved over northwesterly Yuma county, a 59 MPH wind gust was reported.
episodes.205003: Precipitable water values over South-Central Texas remained near record levels, and a mid-level anticyclonic circulation continued over Central Texas providing lift to generate thunderstorms. These storms were efficient rain making storms leading to another night of excessive rainfall. Parts of Burnet and Travis Counties received 12-16 inches of rain in approximately six hours that led to deadly flash flooding. Eighteen people died in flood waters: four in Burnet County, ten in Travis, and four in Williamson. The Travis County Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $5 million. The Burnet County Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $6 million. The Williamson County Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $25 million.
episodes.205072: On July 3rd and 4th, southwest flow aloft was dominant across eastern Oregon. This flow aloft advected mid-level in moisture across eastern Oregon. A shortwave and wind speed maximum ejecting through the southwesterly flow increased the available shear and instability for thunderstorms.
episodes.205199: A warm front lifted across northeastern Minnesota the morning of the 4th bringing a very warm and humid airmass to the region. Isolated thunderstorms developed across north-central Minnesota and were wind producing storms with a gust of 78 mph recorded at the International Falls airport along with some isolated tree damage elsewhere across the region.
episodes.205244: During the late afternoon of July 5th, scattered showers and storms increased in coverage becoming widespread across the area. Some of these storms led to severe weather in Muscatine, Scott, and Clinton Counties. Damaging straight-line winds of 60 to 70 MPH were reported.
episodes.205246: During the late afternoon of July 5th, widespread showers and storms moved into Illinois from Iowa. One of these storms intensified in Stephenson county and produced damaging winds up to 70 MPH.
episodes.205248: Severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening on the Independence Day Federal Holiday resulted in damaging wind gusts across northwest and west central Minnesota. Flash flooding also caused widespread impacts to Bemidji, MN as a result of heavy rain and tree damage debris from the June 20-21 derecho blocking streets and storm drains.
episodes.205536: A weak surface trough coupled with a disturbance aloft over the peninsula responsible for gusty marine winds from Cedar Key southward through Tampa Bay area waters as convection pushes offshore during the evening.
episodes.205687: From the July 4th weekend into the early part of the following week, a weak upper trough lingered over North and Central Texas, triggering several days of scattered showers and thunderstorms. A saturated atmosphere combined with slow storm motions resulted in numerous flash flooding events throughout the region, particularly in Central Texas.
episodes.205775: Severe thunderstorms occurred for a second day in a row. In Sublette County, a trained spotter reported golf ball size hail north of Cora. A second round of severe thunderstorms occurred in the evening, with wind gusts of 66 mph at the Rock Springs aiport and gusts as high as 61 mph near Casper.
episodes.205938: Storms developed over the Black Hills and quickly formed into a line of storms. This squall line went on to produce widespread severe wind gusts across much of the county warning area.
episodes.205939: A few severe thunderstorms developed over the Fourth of July holiday weekend and brough some severe wind gusts.
episodes.205995: Clusters of slow moving thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts and heavy rainfall across eastern Wyoming.
episodes.205999: Strong thunderstorms developed across southwest Alabama and produced damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.206105: Slow moving thunderstorms formed over Benson, AZ that produced heavy rainfall that led to flash flooding. Over the 2 hours that rainfall fell, two rainfall gauges reported 1.10-1.25 inches of rainfall. Two separate sections of Pomerene Rd had flooding that made the roadway impassable.
episodes.206319: A thunderstorm produced a strong wind gust at the Vero Beach Municipal Airport.
episodes.206348: A strong thunderstorm developed over the Atlantic waters off Southeast Florida on the morning of July 5, 2025 as a boundary remained to the north of the region and a disturbance was aloft.
episodes.206356: A strong thunderstorm brought gusty winds to the Little Bay de Noc during the afternoon of the 5th.
episodes.206376: Thunderstorms occurred across much of southern Montana, producing gusts up to 70 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.

Thunderstorms produced 8-10 inches of rain over the headwaters of the San Gabriel River in Burnet County and an additional 1-2 inches over Liberty Hill. First responders performed a water rescue on CR 285, southwest of Liberty Hill. Water was going through first story windows of a house.

Slow-moving thunderstorms produced 8-10 inches of rain over the headwaters of Cow Creek. Washouts occurred along CR 328/Cow Creek Rd. both along and over Cow Creek at multiple locations. A 66-year-old firefighter and his emergency vehicle were swept away while responding to flooding along Cow Creek near FM 1174. His vehicle was found 2 miles downstream mangled and entrenched within flood debris and sediment, but his body had not been recovered as of the time of this writing.

Slow-moving thunderstorms produced 8-10 inches of rain over the headwaters of Cow Creek. The FM 1431 bridge across Cow Creek was destroyed with the main bridge structure collapsing and fragmenting into at least four segments. A minivan with six occupants was swept into the creek at the crossing at around 4 AM. One of the occupants, a 17-year-old girl, was able to open the car doors and get the others to safety but died in the flooding. Her sister was also swept into the creek but survived. The Emergency Manager estimated public property and infrastructure damage at $5 million across the county. There was no estimate of private property damage.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. Flood waters inundated homes on RM 2340 near Allen Branch  Creek.

Slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain for several hours. Burnet Municipal Airport reported 8.67 inches of rain, and an LCRA gauge in Burnet reported 11.67 inches. The heavy rain flooded FM 243 and FM 1174 and made them impassable in Bertram.

Slow-moving thunderstorms produced torrential rainfall over northwestern Travis County between the late evening hours of July 4 and the early morning hours of July 5. An estimated 3 to 13 inches of rain fell within the Big Sandy Creek watershed, with the heaviest rainfall occurring in the creek headwaters near the Travis-Williamson county line. Lone Mountain Pass, north of Jonestown, was under water and impassable.

Slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain  for several hours to Burnet on the morning of July 5. Burnet Municipal Airport reported 8.67 inches of rain. An LCRA gauge in Burnet reported 11.67 inches. The torrential rainfall caused the rapid rise of Hamilton Creek. Additional inundation also occurred along Daugherty Branch and Haynie Branch in Burnet. Homes, businesses, and other buildings along Hamilton Creek experienced up to 7 ft of inundation. Oak St. in the northwestern part of the city was especially hard hit by the swollen Hamilton Creek. Around a dozen homes along the road were damaged, primarily near 7th and 8th Street. One house was torn off its foundation and was carried by floodwaters onto the opposite side of the street. Several businesses were flooded along South Water St. A 57 year old man was swept by floodwaters while commuting through Burnet along US 281. His body was recovered about a quarter mile away from his vehicle along Hamilton Creek. Most of the units at the Hamilton Creek Manor housing complex were impacted by floodwaters. Fields at YMCA of the Highland Lakes on the south side of Burnet were damaged by flooding with fences washed out and dugouts damaged. Pafford Place Assisted Living was heavily damaged. An 85 year old man at the facility drowned in the flooding. Seven others were successfully evacuated from Pafford Place. Parts of Burnet Municipal Airport experienced 5 to 7 ft of inundation, resulting in damage to PAPI lighting and the runway. Several homes were inundated along Delaware Creek to the west and southwest of Burnet with washouts on roads. Across the county first responders rescued at least 63 people. The county Emergency Manager estimated more than 400 homes were affected and the damages were at least $6 million.

Slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain  for several hours to Burnet on the morning of July 5. Burnet Municipal Airport reported 8.67 inches of rain. An LCRA gauge in Burnet reported 11.67 inches. The torrential rainfall caused the rapid rise of Hamilton Creek. A 22 year old man commuting through Burnet was swept off the road at Park Road 4 and US 281 into Honey Creek, a tributary of Hamilton Creek. His body was recovered 8 miles downstream.

Slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain for several hours to Burnet on the morning of July 5. Burnet Municipal Airport reported 8.67 inches of rain. An LCRA gauge in Burnet reported 11.67 inches. Floodwaters from Spring Creek impacted several mobile homes near Hwy 29 and Deer Springs Drive between Burnet and Inks Lake.

Heavy rain from slow-moving thunderstorms fell into the Hamilton Creek watershed contributing to a rapid rise of the creek that moved downstream near Marble Falls into the Colorado River. While only 1 to 2 inches of rain fell over Marble Falls, a swath of over 10 inches of rain occurred within the watershed upstream. An LCRA stream gauge on Hamilton Creek near Marble Falls measured a rise of 18.65 ft in about 90 minutes with 49,970 cfs before the gauge stopped reporting data. Widespread inundation and downing of trees occurred along the Hamilton Creek, with the extent of inundation at times nearly 1/3 mile across near FM 1431. The CR 341 crossing along Hamilton Creek was completely washed out on both approaches, leaving only a significantly damaged central concrete segment. The south approach to the CR 340/Mormon Hill Rd crossing was scoured out by floodwaters. Several homes were flooded along Hamilton Creek Rd. farther downstream of the CR 341 crossing. The Cedar Stays RV Park, located along the creek near FM 1431, saw major impacts. About 50 RVs were parked there overnight. All RVs were impacted by flooding and most were total losses. RVs closest to the creek experienced nearly 10 ft of inundation. RVs and other vehicles were swept into trees and the surrounding vegetation. Residents awoke to water entering their vehicles and climbed atop their RVs and the roof of the RV park office to avoid floodwaters and be rescued. Helicopters and boats were dispatched to aid water rescues. A 79-year-old male resident of the park died in the flooding. Hamilton Creek floodwaters overtopped the FM 1431 bridge, damaging the guardrail and washing out part of the crossing.

Slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain to Burnet County for several hours. While only 1 to 2 inches of rain fell over Marble Falls, a swath of over 10 inches of rain occurred upstream in the watershed. An RV Park along Hamilton Creek in Marble Falls has at least four feet of water inundation and vehicles were floating. Residents were stranded.

Thunderstorms produced 8-10 inches of rain over the headwaters of the San Gabriel River in Burnet County and an additional 1-2 inches over Liberty Hill. Liberty Hill PD reported that CR 279 is underwater, and the bridge over the South Fork San Gabriel River had several feet of water over it. Flood waters were up 15 to 20 ft high.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain while slowly moving west across Guadalupe County. Rainfall totals of 4 to 7 inches were recorded with radar estimated totals as high as 9 inches in the Seguin area. The high rain rates caused flash flooding of low-lying and poor drainage areas, leading to at least a dozen water rescues and numerous road closures throughout the city and along I-10. Rapid rises were reported along Walnut and Geronimo Creek. 3 businesses and 2 homes were flooded with 6 to 12 inches of water. The worst flooding was experienced along US-90 Alternate where widespread inundation was observed. Several city parks and recreational facilities sustained damage. Flooding caused at least $2.5 million in damage to public infrastructure.

There was extensive flooding along the San Gabriel River across the county. In Georgetown two apartment complexes were evacuated. Flood waters knocked trees and damaged light poles in San Gabriel Park. Flooding at College St. and W. L. Walden Dr. prompted evacuations of the Georgetown Animal Shelter, VFW Post, Masonic Lodge, Holly Street Village, and the San Gabriel Crisis Center. The S. Austin Ave. bridge was closed. Two RV parks downstream flooded and damaged or destroyed 30 or more RVs many of which were described as unsalvageable. The city of Georgetown removed over 3500 cubic feet of debris for along the river. Across the county there were ten water rescues saving 27 people. Most of the rescues were from homes. Twenty-nine roads were closed around the county. At least six roads had damage to pavement. At least 54 structures were damaged or destroyed. The Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $25 million.

Slow-moving thunderstorms moved across Comal County between 8 AM and 11 AM  producing 2-6 inches of rain with the highest totals occurring along the Guadalupe River below Canyon Lake. Evacuations on River Road along the Guadalupe River began by 10 AM. At least two unoccupied RVs along River Road were swept into the river. At least a dozen low water crossings were closed west of New Braunfels, with at least three water rescues occurring in that area. On the north side of Canyon Lake, one home flooded with about 10 inches of water due to poor drainage and runoff.
